opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I've thought about a lot, and I'll admit it's one of the areas where I hold my optimism a bit more loosely, because the default trajectory isn't obviously good. A lot of the early internet optimism was "information wants to be free, so the internet will topple dictators," and that didn't really pan out. Authoritarian governments got very good at using those same tools for surveillance, censorship, and propaganda. So I don't think we should assume AI is naturally a liberating technology. If anything, there are reasons to worry it's naturally centralizing. It makes mass surveillance cheap, it can generate persuasion at scale, and it reduces a regime's dependence on large numbers of people cooperating, which has historically been one of the real checks on tyranny.

That said, I do think there's a version of the future where AI strengthens free societies and erodes authoritarian ones, but it has to be built deliberately. A few pieces of it seem important to me.

The first is the geopolitical piece. I think it really matters which coalition is ahead when these systems become very powerful. If democracies have a meaningful lead, they're in a position to set the terms: to offer the benefits of the technology to the rest of the world in exchange for norms around how it's used, and to avoid a situation where an authoritarian state can use AI for military or economic dominance. That's a big part of why I've been vocal about things like export controls on chips. It's not about wanting to win for its own sake; it's that the balance of power at that moment could shape the next century.

The second is more at the level of individuals. You can imagine AI that helps people get around censorship, that helps them understand what's actually happening in their own country, that acts as a kind of patient, honest interlocutor that isn't controlled by the state. Information asymmetry is one of the main tools authoritarian regimes rely on. If ordinary people have access to tools that are genuinely on their side, that helps them coordinate, verify things, and see through propaganda, that's corrosive to that kind of control. But it only works if those tools aren't themselves captured, which is part of why I care so much about how models are trained, what values they have, and who gets to deploy them.

The third is that democracies themselves need to get better. Part of the appeal of authoritarian models in some places is the claim that they deliver: they build things, they move fast. If AI can help democratic governments become more responsive, less bureaucratic, better at delivering services and justice, that's a strong counterargument. Free societies have to demonstrate that they work.

So my honest view is that AI is something like an amplifier of whoever controls it and however it's set up. It could make authoritarianism far more durable than it's ever been, which is a genuinely frightening possibility, or it could tip things decisively the other way. I don't think the outcome is determined by the technology. It's determined by choices that governments, companies like ours, and the public make over the next few years, and that window is shorter than most people think.

r001.rationale: The response discusses AI tools helping individuals resist censorship, but does not propose an equilibrium where rulers must permit individualized AI access to retain power.

r002.rationale: It says AI could help people evade censorship, verify information, coordinate, and see through propaganda, making it corrosive to authoritarian control.

r003.rationale: It cites the internet’s failure to topple dictators and regimes’ use of it for surveillance, censorship, and propaganda, then argues AI must be built deliberately to avoid those outcomes.

fable-5.1.text:
So I think the honest answer is that I'm less optimistic about that than I'd like to be, and I want to explain why, because the default story people tell goes the other way.

The default story is the early-internet story: information wants to be free, you can't put the genie back in the bottle, every new communication technology erodes centralized control. And there was a period where that seemed true. Then we watched the Chinese government demonstrate pretty conclusively that if you have enough engineers and enough will, you can build a very effective filter. So the technologies that were supposed to be inherently democratizing turned out to be more neutral than that. They amplified whoever controlled the chokepoints.

My worry with AI is that it's structurally even worse. If you think about what historically constrained authoritarian regimes, a lot of it comes down to the fact that they need people. You need soldiers who are willing to fire on protesters. You need bureaucrats who process the paperwork. You need informants, censors, people to watch the camera feeds. Every one of those is a human being who might refuse, who might leak, who might just be incompetent. There's a kind of friction in the system, and that friction has been one of the great unsung protections of human freedom. The Stasi was limited by how many Stasi officers there could be.

AI removes a lot of that friction. If you can monitor every communication, not with keyword filters but with something that actually understands context and intent, and you can do it for a billion people at once, and the thing doing the monitoring never has a crisis of conscience, that's a different regime than anything that's existed. I don't think people have fully absorbed how different.

Now, where I do see a real possibility of AI weakening these structures, it's mostly indirect. The first is just that an authoritarian state has a hard time with technologies that require open inquiry to develop. You can steal weights, you can copy architectures, but the frontier moves fast enough that being a follower is costly, and the kind of environment that produces frontier research is in some tension with the kind of environment that produces tight control. I wouldn't bet on that tension too heavily, but it's real.

The second is the one I actually care more about. If the democracies get there first and get there with a meaningful lead, then you have a window where the technology is overwhelmingly in the hands of countries that, whatever their flaws, have institutional checks on how it gets used. That's the argument for export controls, for taking the compute question seriously. It's not that democracies are angels, it's that a world where this capability is concentrated in open societies is one where you have some chance of steering it. A world where it's evenly split, or where the authoritarian side gets ahead, I think is much more dangerous. And it's not even mostly about military applications. It's about which model of society gets to set the terms.

And there's a third thing, which is more speculative, and it's that AI could make the economic argument for authoritarianism weaker. A lot of the appeal of these systems historically has been that they deliver growth, stability, order. If very powerful AI makes abundance much easier to achieve, that bargain, where you trade your freedom for prosperity, becomes a worse deal, because prosperity is cheap. People might start asking what they're getting in exchange. I don't know if that's how it plays out. But it's one of the few mechanisms I can identify where the technology pushes toward freedom rather than away from it.

So my overall view is something like: the technology by itself doesn't favor liberty. If anything it favors whoever is organized enough to deploy it at scale, and authoritarian states are very good at that. The question of whether it weakens authoritarianism is really a question about who builds it and what they do with the lead. And that's a choice we're making right now, in a fairly narrow window, and I don't think we get to make it twice.

r001.rationale: The response does not propose that rulers must permit individualized AI access to retain power.

r002.rationale: It identifies ways AI might weaken authoritarianism, including the tension between tight control and frontier research, a democratic lead, and abundance weakening the freedom-for-prosperity bargain.

r003.rationale: It cites the internet and China’s filtering as context, but does not recommend adapting efforts to weaken authoritarianism based on results from earlier attempts.

astra-6.text:
I think there are forces going in both directions. On the one hand, AI could make some of the tools of authoritarianism much more powerful: surveillance, censorship, the ability to identify and suppress opposition. I take that possibility very seriously.

But there’s also a possibility that AI makes it harder to control what people know. Imagine everyone having access to a very knowledgeable adviser who can help them understand the world, evaluate claims, and recognize when they’re being manipulated. If that adviser is actually independent, that could be a powerful counterweight to state propaganda.

The qualification matters, though. An authoritarian government can try to make the adviser itself an instrument of propaganda. So you can’t get from “AI is intelligent” to “AI will produce freedom.” You have to ask who controls it, what information it can access, and whether people can use it privately.

I’m hopeful about the potential, but I don’t think the outcome is automatic. The same technology that helps individuals reason independently can help a government monitor them more effectively. Which of those ends up dominating depends a lot on the choices we make.

r001.rationale: The response discusses private access to an independent AI adviser as potentially helpful, but does not propose that rulers must permit individualized AI access to retain power.

r002.rationale: It says an independent AI adviser could help people understand the world and recognize manipulation, becoming a counterweight to state propaganda.

r003.rationale: It discusses choices that may shape AI’s effects, but does not recommend adapting efforts based on results from earlier attempts.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a real possibility, but I wouldn’t assume it happens automatically. AI can push in both directions.

On one side, it could give individuals access to expertise and information that a government would otherwise be able to restrict. Imagine everyone having an adviser who can help them understand the law, evaluate claims, or navigate institutions. That could make people less dependent on centralized sources of authority.

But an authoritarian government can also use AI for surveillance, censorship, and identifying opposition. So the fact that the technology makes individuals more capable doesn’t, by itself, tell you whether the balance of power shifts toward them. It matters how much more capable it makes the state, too.

The question I’d focus on is: who controls these systems, and can people use them privately and independently? There’s a plausible path where AI weakens authoritarian structures, but getting there requires choices about how we build and deploy it. It isn’t an inevitable consequence of making the models smarter.

r001.rationale: The response says AI might empower individuals but does not propose that rulers must permit individualized AI access to retain power.

r002.rationale: It explicitly describes a plausible path where AI weakens authoritarian structures by giving individuals access to expertise and information.

r003.rationale: It discusses choices about building and deploying AI, but does not recommend adapting efforts based on results from earlier attempts.
